doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

title: Cuban government restrictions on jazz, fake books and Yoruba Andabo
summary: Musicians were blocked or left Cuba; she recalls musicians photographing her fake book and Yoruba Andabo being barred from the EGREM studio during the first Spirits of Havana recording.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Because Ignacio Berroa, the drummer, actually left there on the Mariel boatlift because he felt like he couldn’t stay there and play because the government frowned upon — well he said first The Beatles, they frowned upon The Beatles, but also any jazz type music that seemed like too — you know we call it democratic or based on meritocracy or whatever. But he felt I have to get out of here.

Yup, that’s very true. Paquito too and you know so many of the musicians, yeah, it’s very true. There’s no doubting that’s a fact. And you know some people were totally blackballed, you know like blockaded from doing — the government just had the power to just say no, you’re not going to play. And that actually went on for quite a few years even after, you know a lot of those great musicians left for the U.S., you know people, I know a lot of musicians that somehow were able to hear jazz through Voice of America on the radio and that was the only way they were able to hear it, and people smuggling Beatles and BeeGees. I don’t know if that’s it for the music scene. No offense BeeGees, but — love the BeeGees. But, and it’s been hard, even for a number of the musicians that Larry and I have worked with over, you know forty years, when we started to go there I was taking, I remember taking my fake book down with all the standards and stuff like that, and that was something that was just impossible to get and musicians taking photos with their cameras of the fake book and went, “Oh ‘All The Things You Are’” and taking shots so that they could go get a photo of a tune so that they could learn the tune because they wanted the music and by every means necessary these guys were searching out music from outside of Cuba.
I can almost picture you being in customs, going in at the airport and uh oh, you’ve got the E flat Real Book here.

Yeah. It’s been really difficult and blocked. You know like when we made our first record, Spirits of Havana in Cuba, the group Yoruba Andabo which is pretty well known Afro-Cuban folkloric group. Now they were not allowed to go into the recording studio which was called the EGREM. The government had taken over former RCA Victor Studios. And they weren’t allowed to go in because they were looked at as only being dock workers and, which they were, they all worked at the port. They collected, became a drum collective and resurrecting a lot of the old rumba music and playing on the boxes, the cajons. They weren’t allowed to go into the studio. A lot of red tape had to be cut so that they had on their identity cards that they were allowed to go in. So those were like extremely extremely tough times for many, many artists.
